target.title: fix(diagnostics-otel): classify model calls as client spans
target.body:
Closes #102017

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators exporting OpenTelemetry traces would see model-provider calls classified as `INTERNAL` unless they enabled the experimental GenAI semantic-convention shape. That hid outgoing model dependencies in trace backends and made provider latency harder to distinguish from in-process work.

## Why This Change Was Made

The model-call span kind was coupled to `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN`, even though that setting should control span naming and provider attributes rather than whether a model request is a client operation. This change keeps model-call spans `CLIENT` in both legacy and experimental naming modes.

Generic tool-execution spans deliberately remain `INTERNAL`: the shared event represents local reads, writes, processes, and remote tools without carrying a reliable remote-execution signal. This follows the scope requested when #102041 was closed and avoids misclassifying local work.

The public OpenTelemetry docs and configuration reference now describe that boundary explicitly.

## User Impact

Trace backends can consistently classify model-provider calls as outgoing client operations without requiring an experimental environment setting. Existing dashboards that filter model spans by `INTERNAL` may need to include `CLIENT`; runtime behavior, configuration, and exported span names are otherwise unchanged.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service.test.ts` — 107 tests passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/qa-otel-smoke.e2e.test.ts` — 28 tests passed.

target.title: fix(cron): keep memory search available with agent overrides
target.body:
Closes #104194

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with global memory-search settings and a partial per-agent `memorySearch` override would lose semantic recall in isolated cron runs. The cron path replaced the complete global object with the partial override, so an index built for an explicit embedding model could be rejected when the runtime fell back to the provider default.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cron defaults builder now keeps `memorySearch` out of its agent-to-defaults flattening, matching the existing `sandbox` boundary. The canonical memory-search resolver remains responsible for merging global defaults with the target agent's override, avoiding both clobbered nested settings and double application.

target.title: feat(control-ui): selection popup with More details and Ask in side chat via /btw
target.body:
Closes #104204

## What Problem This Solves

Digging into a specific phrase of an assistant reply required hand-writing a `/btw` side question: retype the fragment, phrase the question, send. There was no fast path from "I don't understand this part" to an answer, even though the gateway already supports ephemeral side questions end to end.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a Codex-app-style selection popup to the Control UI chat, built entirely on the existing `/btw` machinery. Selecting text inside a chat bubble shows a floating toolbar with two actions: **More details** immediately sends an implicit `/btw Explain "<selection>" from this conversation in more detail.` and the answer arrives as the existing live side result; **Ask in side chat** pre-fills the composer with `/btw Regarding "<selection>": ` so the user types their own question. Because `/btw` sends detached and previously gave zero feedback until `chat.side_result` arrived, the side-result panel now shows a pending "Thinking…" card from the moment the question is sent (also benefiting hand-typed `/btw`). Selection snippets are whitespace-collapsed and capped at 600 chars because `/btw` questions are single-line. Non-goals: no popup on TUI/external channels, no "Add to task" action, no change to `/btw` server semantics.

## User Impact

In the Control UI you can highlight any part of a chat message and either get an instant contextual explanation (never written to session history) or start a pre-quoted side question in the composer. Sending `/btw` now shows immediate pending feedback instead of silence.

## Evidence

- Live-tested against a scratch gateway from this branch (vite dev UI + `chat.send`/`chat.side_result` roundtrip with a real Anthropic model): selection popup appears over the bubble, More details shows the pending card instantly and the BTW side result replaces it; Ask in side chat pre-fills the composer draft `/btw Regarding "trust validation, s": ` and the typed question returns a side result labeled "Not saved to chat history".
- New unit tests: `ui/src/lib/chat/side-question.test.ts` (snippet collapsing/caps, command/draft builders), `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-selection-popup.test.ts` (popup show/dismiss, action routing, bubble scoping), pending-card render coverage in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-composer.test.ts`.

target.title: fix(googlechat): add timeout to Google auth fetch requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Google Chat auth requests made through `createGoogleAuthFetch()` — the shared fetch implementation injected into Gaxios as the Google auth transport — had no request deadline. Token refresh, cert fetch, and any other HTTP auth operation could wait indefinitely when a Google auth endpoint accepted the connection but never responded.

## Why This Change Was Made

- A 30s request timeout (`GOOGLE_AUTH_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`) is added to the `fetchWithSsrFGuard` call inside `createGoogleAuthFetch()`. This matches the deadline used by Vertex ADC (#102050), Chutes OAuth (#102026), MiniMax OAuth (#102862), Google Chat cert fetch (#102924), and every other control-plane auth path.
- Any caller-provided `AbortSignal` is extracted from the sanitized init and passed as the guard's `signal` parameter so `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` composes it with the 30s deadline.
- The existing SSRF policy, dispatcher routing, body-size limit, response buffering, and release lifecycle are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

Reworked the proof to exercise the **real** `fetchWithSsrFGuard` (no guard mock) against a real `node:http` loopback server, mirroring the pattern used by the merged MiniMax OAuth timeout proof (#102862): the production 30s deadline scheduled by `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` is captured and fired **only after the loopback server confirms the request genuinely arrived**, so the stall is proven without wall-clock races.

- The guarded request keeps the real SSRF hostname allowlist satisfied (`https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`); only `globalThis.fetch` is redirected onto the hanging loopback origin so the guard's composed timeout signal rides the real request.
- **Stalled request** → firing the captured production deadline aborts the in-flight request and `createGoogleAuthFetch()` rejects with `AbortError`/`TimeoutError`.
- **Earlier caller abort** → an external `AbortSignal.abort()` before the 30s deadline preempts the still-pending deadline and rejects with `AbortError`.
- **Mutation-checked**: with the captured deadline *not* fired, the stalled request never rejects on its own (stays pending past a 2s sentinel); only firing the real deadline (or aborting the caller) rejects it.

### Redacted exact-head runtime output

Exact head: `3deb577e65464ef264decfee4ef013f8eae66e13` (the proof test file is byte-identical to the captured run below; the follow-up commit on this head only fixes eslint in the sibling `google-auth.runtime.test.ts`).

Command:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/googlechat/src/google-auth.runtime.proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

Output (real guard, real loopback server, production deadline fired after receipt):

```
 ✓ google-auth.runtime.proof.test.ts > real guard proof >
     times out a stalled Google auth request through the real production guard  6963ms
 ✓ google-auth.runtime.proof.test.ts > real guard proof >
     rejects when the caller aborts before the 30s deadline through the real production guard  13ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

Mutation control — same test with the captured deadline **not** fired (proves the request genuinely hangs, i.e. the rejection above comes from the real deadline and nothing else):

```
 × times out a stalled Google auth request through the real production guard  10250ms
   → expected stalled Google auth request to reject, got pending
```

Full suite (no regression):

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/googlechat/src/google-auth.runtime.test.ts
      Tests  23 passed (23)
```

### Evidence

- `oxlint extensions/googlechat/src/google-auth.runtime.proof.test.ts` → clean.
- `git diff --check` → clean; `git diff --name-only` confirms **no `pnpm-lock.yaml`** in the diff.
- Hosted **Real behavior proof** workflow on this exact head: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29142396946 → success.
- Hosted CI on this exact head: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29142397634.
- What was **not** tested: live Google OAuth endpoints — no live Google Cloud credentials were available. The hang is reproduced with a real local HTTP server, not the real third-party service.

### Regression tests

| Test | What it proves |
|------|------|
| `times out a stalled Google auth request through the real production guard` | Real `fetchWithSsrFGuard` (unmocked) + real loopback server → firing the captured production 30s deadline aborts the in-flight request → `AbortError`/`TimeoutError` |
| `rejects when the caller aborts before the 30s deadline through the real production guard` | Real guard composes the caller signal; an earlier caller abort preempts the still-pending 30s deadline → `AbortError` |
| `passes a 30s timeout deadline to guarded Google auth fetches` | `timeoutMs` is 30_000 in the guard call |
| `forwards a caller AbortSignal so the guard composes it with the deadline` | Caller signal is passed through to `fetchWithSsrFGuard.signal` |

target.title: Bound Codex session metadata reads
target.body:
## Summary

- cap retained Codex session-metadata lines at 256 KiB while indexing local cost-usage JSONL
- drain every 64 KiB `FileHandle` read in its own autorelease pool so discarded chunks do not accumulate
- skip oversized or malformed metadata records, then recover a later valid `session_meta` record
- cover an incrementally written 8 MiB record, the exact 256 KiB boundary, and regenerate the parser hash

## Why

The metadata pre-scan previously appended input until it found a newline. A damaged or exceptionally large JSONL line therefore grew both the explicit line buffer and autoreleased read-chunk storage in proportion to the record size. The scanner now holds at most the configured line limit plus the current fixed-size read chunk and releases discarded chunks promptly.

This is availability hardening adjacent to #1999. It does not establish or claim that report's root cause.

Fixes #2037.

## Summary
- reparse changed Pi session files so file-level cumulative usage detection stays stable as logs grow
- group Pi assistant usage samples by provider, model, and turn-like lineage, then convert cumulative-looking monotonic sequences into deltas
- prefer request/message IDs before task IDs so a shared task ID cannot collapse independent requests into one cumulative lineage
- keep samples without a lineage raw, and bump the Pi cost formula fingerprint so old overcounted cache entries rebuild

## Tests
- `swift test --filter PiSessionCostScannerTests` - 20 tests passed
- `make check` - passed; existing missing-translation warnings only
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` - clean
- `make test` - not green locally: `AdaptiveRefreshTimerTests` cancels `menu open advances a long idle timer during refresh without postponing an earlier tick` after 30s before reaching the scanner shard; isolated `swift test --skip-build --no-parallel --filter AdaptiveRefreshTimerTests` reproduces the same failure outside this diff

## Risk
Cumulative detection is guarded to large monotonic sequences where the raw sum is at least 3x the final sample and differs by at least 1M tokens. Ordinary small increasing samples, large monotonic samples without a shared lineage, and large rows with unique request IDs under one task ID remain raw/additive.

Review focus: whether the lineage keys cover the current Ultra fork/replay rows without being too broad for ordinary Pi sessions.

target.title: Fix stranded menu scroll after a manual refresh clears a provider error
target.body:
Fixes #2046.

## Problem

When a provider error (red multi-line banner in the top card) is present and the user clicks the persistent **Refresh** row, the refresh updates the open menu's cards in place — but a taller-than-screen tracked menu is left anchored mid-scroll: the viewport never returns to the top, and closing + reopening the menu is the only recovery.

## Fix (rev 3 — addresses both ClawSweeper findings)

Run a **viewport restore directly from the manual-refresh completion path**, bound to **the menu that initiated the refresh**: `refreshMenuProviderNow` captures the initiating menu's identity when the refresh starts, and completion restores only that same menu if it is still open, non-hosted, and dirty — one main-actor turn later so the unfrozen card layout settles.

- **Rev 2** (P1): the first revision armed a pending intent consumed only by an open-menu rebuild, but explicit store actions intentionally defer visible parent rebuilds while the menu is tracking — so the intent never fired on the reported flow and could linger for an unrelated later rebuild. The restore now executes from `startManualRefresh`'s completion with no pending state and no interaction with the rebuild path.
- **Rev 3** (P2): completion no longer scans all open dirty menus. Shared refresh invalidation dirties every open root menu, so a menu opened and scrolled while another menu's refresh was in flight could have been yanked to the top. The restore is keyed to the initiating menu ID captured at start; the menu-switch scenario has a dedicated regression test.

Background data ticks never take this path, so they can never move a viewport the user is reading.

## How the scroll repair works (probed on macOS 26.2)

Standalone AppKit probes against the view-based menu implementation (tall menu of custom-view rows, mutated and scrolled while tracking) established:

- A tracked menu is `NSPopupMenuWindow` → `NSMenuScrollView` (a real `NSScrollView`) → `NSClipView` → `NSTableViewBackedMenuRepresentation`, plus two arrow `NSImageView` strips.
- Row views are **recycled** once they scroll offscreen (`item.view` detaches; `enclosingScrollView` goes nil), so the shared scroll view is resolved through whichever item view is currently attached (`attachedMenuScrollView(in:)`).
- The offset is read and corrected with public API only: `NSView.enclosingScrollView`, `NSClipView.scroll(to:)`, `NSScrollView.reflectScrolledClipView(_:)`. The repair runs inside `performMenuMutationWithoutAnimation` and no-ops when the menu is not scrolled, not oversized, closed, or has no attached window.
- The flipped/non-flipped top-offset math is a pure helper (`menuViewportTopOffset`) with unit coverage.

## Verification

- `make test` — full suite green.
- `make check` — SwiftFormat + SwiftLint --strict clean.
- `swift test --filter StatusMenuViewportRestoreTests` — 9 tests.
- `swift test --filter StatusMenuOpenRefreshTests` — 31 tests green (the deferral baseline the review cited; this fix no longer interacts with the rebuild path at all).
- **End-to-end state test through the production path**: `manual refresh completion restores the open dirty menu viewport end to end` drives `performPersistentRefreshAction(in:)` (the same entry the persistent Refresh row and ⌘R use) on an open tracked menu and asserts the restore fires after completion **without any parent rebuild landing** (the test also asserts the menu is still dirty afterwards, i.e. the deferral behavior the review cited is preserved and the restore no longer depends on a rebuild).
- **Menu-switch regression test**: `menu opened during another menus in-flight refresh is never restored` starts a gated refresh from menu A, closes A, opens menu B mid-flight, completes the refresh, and asserts B is dirty from shared invalidation yet never restored. Companion negatives: a clean initiating menu is not restored; an initiating menu closed mid-flight gets no restore; background rebuilds never restore.

## Fresh-bundle proof status

I attempted the requested fresh-bundle recording and hit a data-safety wall I don't want to work around dishonestly: this machine is my daily driver with a live CodexBar install, and a debug bundle resolves the real user home for provider detection, local cost logs, and Codex auth — so even under an isolated `$HOME` the "synthetic" instance surfaces my real accounts and usage, and seeding `~/.codexbar/config.json` with synthetic providers would also reconfigure the live install. Producing the recording safely needs a clean macOS user account, which I'll set up if you want the video before merging.

Reproducible recipe (clean user account or sandbox machine): `./Scripts/package_app.sh debug` → launch → Debug pane → Error Simulation → set a multi-line error on Claude → make the menu taller than the screen (several providers or stacked token accounts) → open menu, scroll to the bottom, ⌘R → on this branch the viewport re-anchors at the top with the recovered header visible; on `main` it stays stranded.

No keychain access, no provider I/O, UI-layer only. CHANGELOG left untouched per house practice.

Suggested release-note line, if useful: *Menu: re-anchor the open menu at the top after a manual refresh, so a taller-than-screen menu is never stranded mid-scroll once a provider error banner clears; background refreshes never move the viewport.*

target.title: fix(codex): preserve UTF-16 pairs in tool output delta truncation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Codex streaming tool output display renders a corrupted glyph ("�") when a non-BMP character (emoji like 😀) straddles the 8,000-character progress-message truncation boundary. The raw `.slice(0, remainingChars)` on the emitted delta cuts at a UTF-16 code-unit boundary — when `remainingChars` lands on the HIGH surrogate of a surrogate pair, the truncated progress message carries a dangling `\uD83D` that corrupts the rendered output in the chat transcript.

## Why This Change Was Made

`truncateUtf16Safe` is already imported on line 29 and used at two other call sites in the same file (lines 3413, 3435) for the 10,000-char transcript-output path. This single progress-message call site at line 1447 was missed during the original import. The fix reuses the canonical helper — no new abstraction, no new import.

## User Impact

Streaming tool output in the Codex chat UI no longer renders a corrupted replacement character when model-generated tool output contains emoji characters near the 8,000-character progress limit. ASCII-only output is unaffected.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** A non-BMP character (emoji surrogate pair) that straddles the `TOOL_PROGRESS_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS` (8,000) boundary in the Codex event projector's `handleOutputDelta` progress-message path must not produce a lone surrogate in the emitted transcript text.

**Real environment tested:** Node.js v22.22.0, x64, linux, OpenClaw checkout at `2d0d06d3f1`

### Evidence after fix — standalone runtime proof

A standalone Node.js script (`proof-codex-projector-runtime.mts`) imports the real `CodexAppServerEventProjector` class directly from `extensions/codex/src/app-server/event-projector.ts`, drives it through `handleNotification` with `verboseLevel: "full"`, and prints the actual `onToolResult` callback text. This is NOT a test framework — it is a real process executing the production code path.

```
── [Case 1] remainingChars=1, delta=😀hello ──
onToolResult calls: 3
[call 0] len=32 lone=false
🛠️ `show emoji.txt (workspace)`
---
[call 1] len=8019 lone=false
🛠️ Bash
```txt
aaaa...aaaa
```
---
[call 2] len=37 lone=false
🛠️ Bash
```txt
...(truncated)...
```
---
── [Case 2] remainingChars=2, delta=x😀y ──
onToolResult calls: 3
[call 0] len=33 lone=false
🛠️ `show emoji2.txt (workspace)`
---
[call 1] len=8018 lone=false
🛠️ Bash
```txt
aaaa...aaaa
```
---
[call 2] len=39 lone=false
🛠️ Bash
```txt
x
...(truncated)...
```
---

=== RUNTIME PROOF COMPLETE ===
node=v22.22.0
No lone surrogates in any emitted progress text.
Fix confirmed: truncateUtf16Safe in production projector.
```

**Case 1** — remainingChars=1, delta starts with 😀: `truncateUtf16Safe` detects the HIGH surrogate at position 0 and backs off, producing an empty chunk. The progress message is `...(truncated)...` — clean, no surrogate bytes.

**Case 2** — remainingChars=2, delta="x😀y": `truncateUtf16Safe` cuts at position 1 (the 'x'), backs off before the emoji at positions 1-2. The progress message is `x\n...(truncated)...` — clean, no surrogate bytes.

### Negative control (pre-fix behavior reproduced)

Same standalone script, same environment. `event-projector.ts` reverted to `origin/main` (`.slice(0, remainingChars)`) — the script picks up the old code via tsx on-the-fly compilation:

```
── [Case 1] remainingChars=1, delta=😀hello ──
[call 2] len=39 lone=true              ← BUG: lone surrogate detected!
🛠️ Bash
```txt
�                                     ← U+D83D HIGH surrogate, corrupted glyph
...(truncated)...
```
---

target.title: RFC: add local adaptive-refresh replay tooling
target.body: ## Decision requested This RFC asks whether upstream should own a local replay harness for Adaptive refresh and, if so, whether the pure replay tools should be separated from runtime trace collection and the coding-activity probe. It does not change the production policy or make Adaptive the default. The decision record in #1739 requires measured evidence before a default change, and #1861 shipped the current opt-in policy. This branch adds tooling to collect and audit that evidence. Refs #1739 and #1861. ## What is in the branch - `AdaptiveReplayKit`, a Foundation-only library for parsing traces, replaying policies, segmenting unobserved gaps, calculating metrics, and auditing recorded schedule decisions. - `AdaptiveReplayCLI`, a thin command-line wrapper around the library. - An off-by-default app recorder for policy decisions, menu opens, refresh completions, and accepted or rejected timer-advance evaluations. - A shadow-mode coding-activity probe that reads metadata from recent local Codex and Claude Code transcripts. Its signal is never passed to the production policy. - A replay-only candidate that caps unconstrained decisions at five minutes while recent coding activity is present. ## Diff shape Relative to `main`, this is 32 files with 4,147 insertions and 55 deletions. It is a large review surface, so the table separates runtime wiring from the offline harness and its tests. | Surface | Files | Insertions / deletions | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Feature tests | 10 | +1,932 / -0 | | Offline replay library and CLI | 13 | +1,619 / -1 | | App wiring, recorder, and activity probe | 6 | +417 / -6 | | Docs | 2 | +132 / -6 | | Keychain test isolation | 1 | +47 / -42 | The keychain test change wraps an existing suite in no-UI test overrides so the full validation does not read real credentials; its net change is five lines. If upstream wants a smaller sequence, the natural split is replay kit and CLI, runtime recording, then the activity probe and replay-only candidate. ## Local data boundary Tracing is disabled unless the `adaptiveRefreshTraceEnabled` defaults key is set. When enabled, the app appends JSONL records in its Application Support directory. The writer has a hard 10 MiB cap and stops before a record would exceed it; it does not rotate, truncate, or upload the file. The activity probe reads file metadata only: modification time, creation time, size, and the number of recently modified transcripts. It does not read transcript contents or store file paths, project names, account information, credentials, provider responses, or menu content. There is no network or analytics path for these records. The raw trace used below remains local and is not part of this PR. The decision record now proposes the exact file location, manual disable/delete commands, and a one-traced-process-per-file constraint. There is no retention or deletion UI; accepting that boundary is one of the decisions requested by this RFC. ## Replay evidence The frozen single-machine trace contains 1,780 records (SHA-256 `b1e4aa33180b7c177293eb9ed16b45e24e026d259600fba2b1b67b931b904f0b`). The legacy-gap heuristic split it into 28 observed segments and excluded 26.10 hours of unobserved wall time. This is not a causal classification: the trace cannot distinguish sleep or reboot from a long refresh or event-loop stall. Activity metadata was available for 462 of 733 recorded decisions. Of those 462 samples, 185 were inside the five-minute active window. | Policy | Simulated refreshes | Per observed 24h | Simulated advances | Unconstrained active over 5m | Menu staleness p50 / p95 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Current Adaptive | 694 | 143.47 | 53 | 4 / 145 | 142s / 1093s | | Activity-cap candidate | 696 | 143.88 | 53 | 0 / 145 | 139s / 1093s | | Fixed 5m | 1,383 | 285.90 | 0 | 0 / 99 | 150s / 281s | On this trace, current Adaptive scheduled 49.8% fewer simulated refreshes than the fixed five-minute baseline. The replay-only candidate added two refreshes, removed the four active-delay violations, and reduced p50 menu staleness by three seconds. It did not improve p95. The fixed five-minute baseline had a p95 menu staleness of 281 seconds, compared with 1,093 seconds for both Adaptive variants. This trace therefore supports the scheduled-work reduction but does not support making Adaptive the default. The frozen trace predates the new evaluation event. It contains 46 recorded timer advances and zero timer-advance evaluations, so it cannot validate accepted versus rejected live comparisons. A short instrumented run of the equivalent pre-rebase patch series produced two evaluation records, one accepted decision, and zero payload, decision, or menu-link mismatches. That checks the audit path; it is not additional statistical evidence. These numbers count simulated refreshes and observed menu staleness on one machine. They do not measure battery savings, user time saved, provider API requests, or cost. ## Validation Exact candidate: `2d43edbb781fa520357c75fd6938f68d55e93bc4` - `make check` passed, including SwiftFormat and strict SwiftLint. - `make test` passed all 604 selections across 51/51 groups. - Focused replay, parser, trace-recording, segmentation, audit, and activity runs passed 83 tests in 10 suites. This includes the byte-cap/oversized-record cases and one-to-one menu/evaluation linkage. - `swift build --product AdaptiveReplayCLI` passed. - JSON schema smoke checks passed for raw-wall-clock and segmented runs, including audit validity and segmentation provenance. - `CODEXBAR_SIGNING=adhoc ./Scripts/package_app.sh debug` produced a bundle for this exact commit; `codesign --verify --deep --strict` passed. ## Known limitations - The measured trace comes from one machine. - Legacy gap segmentation is heuristic, not causal. - The raw trace is intentionally not published. - Older frozen records cannot audit rejected timer-advance evaluations. - There is no retention or deletion UI yet. - Trace writes and the 10 MiB boundary are serialized within one process; concurrent traced instances sharing the file are unsupported. - This evidence makes no battery, elapsed-user-time, API-request, cost, or default-policy claim. ## Review questions 1. Should the pure replay kit and CLI live in this repository? 2. Should runtime trace recording be reviewed separately? 3. Is the stat-only coding-activity probe acceptable upstream, or should it remain out of tree? 4. What retention and deletion contract is required before persistent traces can ship? This PR does not propose a new production policy, persistent analytics, a default change, or use of the activity signal at runtime.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
